name: MCP1825S-3302E_DB
title: 500 mA LDO regulator for low output voltages, with low quiescent current (MCP1825 / MCP1825S)
summary: A CMOS low-dropout linear regulator for loads up to 500 mA from a 2.1 V to 6.0 V input, with outputs from 0.8 V to 5.0 V, about 120 µA of quiescent current and 210 mV typical dropout at full load. It is stable with a 1 µF ceramic output capacitor and has current limiting and thermal shutdown. The 5-lead MCP1825 adds a shutdown input and either a delayed power-good output (fixed versions) or an adjust pin; the 3-lead MCP1825S, such as the 3.3 V MCP1825S-3302E/DB in SOT-223, is a plain fixed regulator.
key_figures: 210 mV typ, 350 mV max at 500 mA

notes: Code layout: device, two-digit output voltage code, extra feature code (0 = fixed), tolerance code (2 = 2.5 %), temperature code (E = -40 °C to +125 °C), then /package code and an optional qualification suffix.
A T after the device name (MCP1825T, MCP1825ST) orders tape and reel; the rest of the code is unchanged.
Package codes: AB = TO-220 3-lead, AT = TO-220 5-lead, EB = DDPAK 3-lead, ET = DDPAK 5-lead, DB = SOT-223 3-lead, DC = SOT-223 5-lead.
For the ADJ output code the extra feature and tolerance digits are dropped (MCP1825-ADJE/xx); the adjustable output exists only in the 5-lead packages.
Qualification suffix: none = standard part; VAO = AEC-Q100 automotive qualified.
Output voltages outside the seven standard codes are available on request from the factory.

circuits.title: MCP1825 fixed output voltage (1.8 V)
circuits.description: A 1.8 V fixed MCP1825 run from a 2.3 V to 2.8 V input, giving 1.8 V at up to 500 mA. C1 decouples the input and C2 holds the output stable; R1 pulls the open-drain power-good output up to the regulated rail, and an on/off logic signal drives SHDN.

circuits.title: MCP1825 adjustable output voltage (1.2 V)
circuits.description: The adjustable MCP1825 set to 1.2 V at up to 500 mA from a 2.1 V to 2.8 V input. R1 (40 kΩ, output to ADJ) and R2 (20 kΩ, ADJ to ground) divide the output down to the 0.41 V the ADJ pin regulates to; the divider node is also brought out as VADJ. C1 and C2 are the input and output capacitors, and SHDN takes the on/off signal.

operation.text: The MCP1825 comes in 5-lead TO-220, DDPAK and SOT-223 packages with a shutdown input; its fixed versions add a power-good output and its adjustable version uses that pin as ADJ, setting 0.8 V to 5.0 V with two resistors. The MCP1825S is the 3-lead fixed-output version (VIN, GND, VOUT) with neither shutdown nor power-good. Standard fixed outputs are 0.8, 1.2, 1.8, 2.5, 3.0, 3.3 and 5.0 V; the parts pass AEC-Q100 reliability testing.

A PMOS pass transistor sits between VIN and VOUT. An error amplifier compares a reference with the output, fed back through ADJ/SENSE on the adjustable part and through an internal divider on fixed parts, and controls the pass transistor through a driver that carries the current limit and shutdown. Undervoltage lockout, overtemperature sensing and soft-start act on the driver and reference. On the 5-lead fixed parts a comparator at 92 % of VREF, followed by a fixed delay, drives PWRGD.

At least 500 mA is guaranteed, and there is no minimum load: the output stays in regulation down to 0 mA. If an overload pulls the output under 0.7 V (normally a short), the output current is limited to 1.2 A typical. In a milder overload the regulator can supply up to about 1.5 A, which it must not do continuously; pulsed loads whose average is 500 mA or less are acceptable. A sustained overload can also trip the thermal shutdown.

The output needs at least 1 µF to be stable, and up to 22 µF is recommended; more capacitance improves transient response and ripple rejection. Ceramic X7R or X5R parts are preferred for size, cost and robustness and their ESR is well inside the needed range (a 1 µF X7R 0805 is about 50 mΩ). Tantalum and aluminium electrolytic capacitors also work if their ESR is 1 Ω or less, though aluminium electrolytics are not advised below -25 °C. Place the capacitor close to VOUT.

The regulator needs a low-impedance source. With a battery supply, or more than about 10 inches of wiring to the source, fit 1.0 µF to 4.7 µF at VIN; 1 µF to 10 µF suits most uses. For load steps the input capacitor supplies the fast current, so it should match or exceed the output capacitor; a larger one also reduces high-frequency noise and the effect of supply-line inductance. Place it close to VIN.

GND carries only the quiescent current, so it needs no heavy trace, but it should go to a quiet ground for best ripple rejection and noise. With a switching or noisy input, connect GND at the output capacitor's return. Ground planes cut inductance and voltage spikes under fast load steps. At high currents near the 2.1 V minimum input, trace drops between source and VIN can pull the input low enough to trip the undervoltage lockout.

SHDN is active low and its threshold scales with VIN: 30 % of VIN typical, with 45 % (high) and 15 % (low) as the limits over temperature. Low-going pulses up to 400 ns are ignored; a longer low puts the part in shutdown, where it draws 0.1 µA typical and PWRGD is pulled low at once. On a rising edge a 30 µs delay runs before the output starts; a low during that delay restarts it. Soft-start then ramps the output from 0 V, so the total turn-on time TOR is about 100 µs (30 µs plus a 70 µs ramp).

PWRGD is an open-drain output, held low while the output is below the threshold (92 % of nominal typical) plus its hysteresis (2 % typical, 3 % maximum). Once the output passes that level a fixed 110 µs delay (TPG) runs and PWRGD is released. A falling output is detected after a 170 µs delay, which keeps short output transients from toggling the pin. It can be pulled up to any voltage up to VIN and sinks 1.2 mA with VPWRGD under 0.4 V maximum. Coming out of shutdown, PWRGD rises TPG after the 30 µs delay and 70 µs ramp of TOR.

Dropout is taken where the output has fallen 2 % from its value at VR + 0.5 V of headroom; it is 210 mV typical at 500 mA. The input range is 2.1 V to 6.0 V. An undervoltage lockout holds the output off until VIN rises to 2.00 V typical and keeps it on until VIN falls to 1.82 V typical, so the dropout figure does not apply to outputs below 1.8 V.

When the junction reaches about 150 °C the output turns off, and it turns back on by itself once the junction cools to about 140 °C. If dissipation stays too high the part cycles off again. Junction temperature follows from dissipation, ambient temperature and the package's thermal resistance; the maximum continuous junction temperature is +125 °C.
The TO-220 and DDPAK packages have an exposed tab at ground potential that can carry a heat sink. The ground pin draws only the quiescent current, 120 µA typical.

θJA values follow the EIA/JEDEC JESD51 test method and board; on a real board θJA depends on copper area and thickness among other things. Application note AN792 covers working out how much power a small package can dissipate.
